intro: After the funeral march, a ländler in three offers a gentler kind of movement. It returns twice, each time changed: a flowing cello line enriches one return, while plucked strings give the last a new articulation.
question: How can the same dance return with a different character?

cues.title: A dance after the march
cues.text: The Andante begins in A♭ major and 3/8 time. Strings introduce a ländler, a dance in three whose phrasing differs from the preceding funeral march. Mahler marks it “very leisurely” and “never hurry”.
cues.evidence: Full score p. 57: Andante moderato, Sehr gemächlich, Nie eilen, A♭-major key signature and 3/8 metre.

cues.title: Several voices in the strings
cues.text: Follow the melody without losing the answering inner parts. The strings divide and exchange material, so a small orchestral force can contain more than one line worth following.
cues.evidence: Full score pp. 57–58 gives divided strings and melodic responses. The report places this within the opening restrained span; individual exchanges are not aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Triplets change the surface
cues.text: The contrasting episode replaces the dance’s more varied rhythm with running triplets. These are three notes fitted into a beat: the surface can become busier while the underlying movement remains unhurried.
cues.evidence: Full score p. 58, rehearsal 3: minor-key triplets, Nicht eilen, Sehr gemächlich. Onset activity increases in the 1:15–1:55 region; the first triplet is not precisely timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A summer at Steinbach
cues.text: Mahler drafted the Andante during the summer of 1893 at Steinbach am Attersee. The dated draft is 30 July, close to the work on the scherzo and the orchestral version of the fish-sermon song.
cues.evidence: Mahler Foundation manuscript chronology records the Andante draft on 30 July 1893 and neighbouring scherzo/song dates: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-history/

cues.title: The episode loses its force
cues.text: The first contrasting span withdraws sharply after its crest. Listen for the triplet motion becoming less prominent as the music prepares the dance’s return.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls from −14 dB at 2:20 to −35 dB at 2:35 and about −45 dB at 2:50. The score supplies the triplet-to-ländler comparison.

cues.title: A new line below
cues.text: On the ländler’s first return, the cellos add a flowing countermelody beneath the familiar upper-string material. Try following the lower tune for a phrase: the return is an added conversation, not a literal repeat.
cues.evidence: Full score pp. 61–62, and the Mahler Foundation’s movement account, identify the cello counterline. The 3:02 novelty peak and renewed A♭-centred span support this provisional return region.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: From manuscript to print
cues.text: The symphony’s full score appeared in print in February 1897, more than a year after its complete premiere. Hofmeister published the first edition; the rights passed to Josef Weinberger the following month. The early performances had depended on manuscript scores and parts.
cues.evidence: Mahler Foundation, manuscript parts prepared by January 1895, first full-score edition in February 1897 and transfer of publishing rights in March: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-history/

cues.title: The contrast returns enlarged
cues.text: The second triplet episode is much more forceful than its first appearance. Listen for the same kind of rhythmic motion taking on a different scale when the orchestral weight increases.
cues.evidence: The score expands the contrasting material. The report jumps from −29.9 dB at 4:25 to −6.8 at 4:30, with novelty at 4:30 and 4:34.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A broad central climax
cues.text: The movement’s largest sustained crest occupies this central region. Compare it with the restrained opening: the dance movement has made room for an orchestral interruption far heavier than its first phrases suggested.
cues.evidence: All five listed loudest windows occur between 4:30 and 5:05. The strongest novelty peak at 5:14 accompanies the subsequent change of level and texture.

cues.title: Melody above continuous motion
cues.text: In the expanded episode, listen separately to the sustained upper phrases and the running figures below them. The accompaniment can keep moving while a melody stretches across several beats.
cues.evidence: Full score pp. 70–71 places sustained flute, horn and violin lines above divided-string triplets. This is representative scoring within the broad second episode, not an exact bar alignment.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Heard before the complete symphony
cues.text: The Andante was among the three movements Mahler conducted in Berlin on 4 March 1895. The complete five-movement symphony was first heard there in December, adding the alto’s “Urlicht” and the choral finale.

cues.title: The dance returns plucked
cues.text: For the final return, the strings take up the dance pizzicato: plucked rather than bowed. The melody remains recognisable, but its notes now have shorter natural decays, leaving more audible space between attacks.
cues.evidence: Full score p. 73, rehearsal 12 and Tempo I, introduces the pizzicato return. A deep withdrawal around 7:05–7:10 is followed by increased attack activity around 7:30–7:55; timing is passage-level.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Colour without a new tune
cues.text: Piccolo, flute and harp decorate the plucked-string return. Listen for short upper-register touches rather than a new principal theme: orchestration changes how the familiar dance is articulated.
cues.evidence: Full score pp. 73–74 gives piccolo/flute and harp punctuation above pizzicato strings. The note describes that return as a whole; individual decorations are not timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The return broadens again
cues.text: The final dance grows beyond its initially delicate articulation. Follow the increasing weight while keeping its original phrase shape in mind; a transformed return can expand without becoming a new section.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises from roughly −37 dB at 7:20 to −12.5 dB at 8:40, with further crests through 9:10. Score p. 75 marks a broadening within the return.

cues.title: Letting the phrase loosen
cues.text: The closing stretch eases away from that late expansion. Listen for smaller gestures and more space around them, rather than expecting the movement to end with the force of its central climax.
cues.evidence: The report falls from −11.9 dB at 9:10 to −25.2 at 9:35; novelty at 9:12 and 9:42 marks changes within the closing span.

cues.title: A small-scale ending
cues.text: The dance ends by diminishing its sound, not by enlarging the orchestra into another climax. Let the final decay register before the scherzo starts: both movements use a triple metre, but their kinds of motion are very different.
cues.evidence: Level falls from −32 dB at 10:00 to −46 dB at 10:15 and −63 dB at 10:20. The following scherzo’s metre is documented in its score heading.

transitions.title: The dance acquires running triplets
transitions.how: The A♭-major dance gives way to a minor-key passage whose repeated triplets change the surface rhythm. A soft horn figure introduces the new texture; only a few string desks begin the running motion before it spreads through the section. Mahler explicitly says not to hurry, so rhythmic activity should not be confused with a large increase of tempo.
transitions.evidence: Full score p. 58, rehearsal 3: Nicht eilen, Sehr gemächlich; horn and reduced string desks. The report shows increased attacks from 1:15 onward. No unique novelty peak establishes the exact bar, so this boundary remains provisional.

transitions.title: The return adds a second melody
transitions.how: The triplet episode subsides and the ländler returns to A♭ major. Instead of simply repeating the opening, Mahler adds an expressive cello counterline beneath the upper strings. The bass still marks the dance’s foundations, while the new singing line gives the listener another route through familiar harmony.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 61–62 and the Foundation account identify the cello addition. The 2:50 low point, boundary at 3:02 and renewed A♭-centred writing around 3:05–4:05 support the broad return.

transitions.title: A familiar contrast gains weight
transitions.how: The second contrasting episode turns the running triplet material into a much larger orchestral statement. Winds and brass reinforce the strings, and the sustained dynamic level rises sharply. The rhythmic connection makes this a transformed return of B, not an unrelated interruption; its greater weight changes the proportions of the whole movement.
transitions.evidence: The score expands the second triplet episode. The report’s abrupt level rise at 4:30, boundaries at 4:30/4:34 and high plateau through 5:10 strongly support this passage-level boundary.

transitions.title: A withdrawal changes the articulation
transitions.how: The expanded episode dwindles into separated fragments, and the original tempo and A♭-major dance return. Pizzicato spreads through the divided strings, changing the notes from sustained bow strokes to short attacks. Piccolo, flute and harp then add bright punctuation. The form comes home through recognisable phrases, but the sound of that homecoming is newly delicate.
transitions.evidence: Full score p. 73, rehearsal 12 and Tempo I, shows the retreat and pizzicato spread; pp. 73–74 adds flute/piccolo and harp. Report minima at 7:05–7:10 and denser attacks at 7:30–7:55 locate the return approximately.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 2, full score (Hofmeister 1897; Weinberger/Universal Edition reprint)
source.locator: Movement II, pp. 57–79, especially rehearsals 3 and 12. The timeline gives representative passage scoring, not every individual entrance; the performing edition used in 2004 is unknown.

timeline.note: The ländler opens in the strings, with divided inner parts and a measured bass.
The contrasting triplet passage begins with reduced strings and horn, then adds flute, clarinet and harp; those entries are grouped, not individually timed.
The dance returns with an expressive cello countermelody below the upper strings.
Representative expanded-episode scoring: a much heavier wind, brass and string ensemble develops the triplet contrast.
Sustained upper phrases over divided-string triplets, as on pp. 70–71; this is a provisional passage placement.
The final return uses pizzicato strings, with short piccolo/flute and harp decorations added within the passage.

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony anticipates Mahler’s so closely that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony. The cantata Das klagende Lied, written at eighteen and nineteen, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881, and Mahler turned to the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
